item.title: End of COVID-era SNAP emergency food assistance linked to increased child maltreatment rates
item.description: A new study has found that in U.S. counties that ended COVID-19 pandemic-era Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Emergency Allotments, child maltreatment rates went up. The findings from the study in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine suggest that changes to food assistance programs have consequences that extend beyond food security and also affect child and family well-being. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: The first named storm of the North Indian Ocean’s cyclone season made landfall along the coast of Andhra Pradesh. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
item.description: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
item.description: Scientists have defied a long-standing rule of laser physics by generating X-rays with much higher energies than conventional theory predicts. The surprising discovery reveals how two electrons working together can overcome a previously accepted limit, opening new possibilities for quantum research. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Meteors don't just burn up. What really happens is far more violent
item.description: Scientists have uncovered seven surprising stages that space rocks go through as they hurtle toward Earth, revealing that melting and violent fragmentation, rather than simple evaporation, determine their fate. The discovery could help explain why meteorites scatter across the ground and how dangerous asteroids explode in Earth's atmosphere. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Caltech Names Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman as NASA JPL Deputy
item.description: Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Optimistic climate futures for local communities in the UK imagined in a new report
item.description: A new report co-authored by researchers from the University of York and WWF highlights how local communities across the U.K. imagine positive, sustainable, and resilient futures for the places where they live and work. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth
item.description: Scientists have discovered that magma deep inside Earth can store surprising amounts of extra oxygen, potentially revealing a hidden contributor to our planet's oxygen-rich atmosphere. The findings suggest that ancient volcanic eruptions may have helped transform Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago, with implications for understanding life on other planets. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How the Indian Ocean is linked to Europe's early-winter rain and storms
item.description: When we think about Europe's winter weather, the Indian Ocean is probably not the first place we look. We might picture Atlantic storms, cold air arriving from the north or rain sweeping across the Mediterranean. In my research, however, I look at how these familiar weather systems fit into a much larger climate system. My colleagues and I asked whether an ocean thousands of kilometers away could leave a detectable signature on Europe's early winter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The phantom lighthouse: New research explains one of Australia's strangest illusions
item.description: There are two lighthouses on Lady Elliot Island, at the southernmost tip of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. The first was built in 1873, but was decommissioned in 1995 when the second took over the job of warning ships off the reef. Visitors to the island, however, regularly report seeing signs of a third lighthouse. At night the beams of a nonexistent phantom lighthouse are seen far off, shining on the horizon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultrathin metal layer boosts spin-related signals, opening a door to ultralow-power electronics
item.description: Researchers at Kyushu University have found that an ultrathin layer of iridium manganese (IrMn) can improve two spin-related signals in a structure made of a magnetic insulator and a platinum film. By examining how spin currents are generated and absorbed, the team gained insights into how the intermediate layer improves spin transfer. The findings could inform the development of ultralow-power devices for computing and energy harvesting. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Atomic magnetism reveals why iron, but not chromium, can produce ammonia using sunlight
item.description: Two nearly identical materials have completely different chemical behavior. Research teams at the University of Vienna and TU Wien studied catalysts that use the energy of sunlight to produce ammonia. Surprisingly, when the three iron atoms that form tiny triangles in these catalysts are replaced by chromium atoms, the chemical reaction no longer takes place. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ULA's Vulcan rocket is set to return to flight on Friday the 13th
item.description: This Vulcan launch will be the first to utilize a full complement of six solid rocket boosters. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark

item.title: Macromolecular crowding could help build artificial cell systems
item.description: Macromolecular crowding can serve as a design tool for controlling the formation and organization of synthetic DNA droplets, a study from Science Tokyo reveals. Researchers investigated this strategy using DNA nanostars and polymeric crowding agents to mimic the crowded cellular environment. They found that crowding promoted droplet formation and enabled control over droplet size, interactions and organization. The findings could support the development of programmable artificial cell systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular architecture determines tomato plant resistance to its main pest
item.description: An international study investigating why wild tomatoes are more resistant to the tomato leafminer (Phthorimaea absoluta) than cultivated varieties revealed that the secret lies in the spatial structure of a plant defense molecule. The researchers mapped the biochemical origin of this difference and demonstrated that altering four amino acids in a single enzyme is sufficient to alter the structure of the substance and increase its toxicity against the pest. This finding paves the way for creating resistant tomatoes through gene editing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Explaining the difference between brittle and ductile behavior in polymer glasses
item.description: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily. Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Welcomes Vietnam as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
item.description: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space. “Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Shaw

item.title: Q&A: Decoding the cell—a conversation with a computational biologist
item.description: Computational biologist Christina Leslie, Ph.D., has spent nearly two decades at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) building computational tools that help make sense of some of the most complex data in biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chornobyl dog population shows genetic signatures of directional selection
item.description: The latest research on the wild population of dogs in Chornobyl reveals that the genetic differences between these dogs and other similarly isolated dog populations are likely evidence of directional selection, not mutation. The work suggests a potential association between genetic selection and environmental variables and could advance understanding of local adaptation and genomic resilience in contaminated environments. The study appears in Genes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
item.description: Planning a successful trip can be challenging, especially when your destination is in outer space. Even before liftoff, space missions require extraordinary amounts of scientific preparation and data analysis to succeed, which can take years to complete. However, as space agencies race to establish a permanent presence on the moon, using artificial intelligence to combine such information into a single system could make mission planning much more efficient. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Same radical, different paths: X-ray snapshots reveal how neighboring molecules shape its movement
item.description: Chemical reactions have their own "impatient molecules." Unable to stay still even for a moment, they latch onto other molecules indiscriminately. Researchers have now found that even these molecules change where they "sit" and how far they roam depending on who their neighbors are. The findings are expected to help scientists make better medicines and materials by directing reactions only to the desired sites. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon‑stealing spirits
item.description: Stories of wandering spirits and the restless dead were common in the Middle Ages. These ghostly encounters were recorded in a wide variety of medieval literature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rarely seen deep-sea barreleye fish filmed in 4K
item.description: During a recent expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard, MBARI scientists encountered a rarely seen barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma). This sighting is MBARI's 11th observation of this unique deep-sea fish with a transparent head. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Drones could help weather forecasters more accurately predict winter storms
item.description: Weather drones are being tested to help update forecasts of extreme weather more quickly, and could help us prepare earlier for upcoming winter storms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Controlling where gibberellin acts reveals how the plant hormone coordinates root growth
item.description: Plant hormones influence growth and development by acting on specific cells and tissues. However, determining precisely where and when a hormone needs to act has been challenging because conventional hormone treatment generally activates signaling throughout the plant. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an 'extinct' giant crane solved
item.description: Scientists at Bournemouth University (BU) have solved a 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an extinct giant crane that lived in Europe over 20,000 years ago. The work is published in the journal Royal Society Open Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New tissue atlas aims to help AI understand cancer
item.description: How cells are arranged within tissue can reveal as much about disease as the cells themselves. When doctors examine a cancer tumor, for example, they don't just look at which cells are present; they also want to know how those cells are arranged and how they interact with each other. That's because the way cancer cells interact with neighboring immune cells can offer important clues about how a disease develops or responds to treatment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to make way for human development rarely delivers long-term conservation success
item.description: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to protect them from development rarely leads to long-term conservation success, a new UBC-led global review has found. The findings highlight the importance of habitat protection rather than relying on moving animals out of harm's way. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sun's outer magnetic field mapped in 3D for the first time
item.description: A team of researchers has produced the first global, three-dimensional estimates of the sun's magnetic field, including the area beyond the sun's visible edge. This marks a step toward more accurate models of solar activity—and ultimately, better predictions of solar magnetic eruptions, which are the root cause of extreme space weather that can impact critical infrastructure technologies on Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Customizable DNA labels can selectively guide drug carriers to cancer cells
item.description: Cells naturally send tiny packages to one another to share information. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University have developed a simple, low-cost way to turn those packages into drug carriers that can deliver treatments directly to cancer cells, potentially improving effectiveness while reducing side effects. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Humidity can change how smoke pollutants transform after dark
item.description: What happens to smoke particles after sunset can depend strongly on something as familiar as the amount of water in the air. New research from Md. Sohel Rana and Marcelo I. Guzman at the University of Kentucky shows that relative humidity can redirect the chemical pathways involved in the nighttime oxidation of catechol, a phenolic compound associated with biomass burning. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Let nothing be forgotten': Holocaust survivors' memorial books honored lives lost and vibrant hometowns
item.description: My grandmother was a Holocaust survivor from Kostopol, Ukraine. Years after she passed away, I was trying to learn more about her life before the war—something I knew very little about. When I found a book called "Sefer Kostopol"—Hebrew for "Book of Kostopol"—I hoped to find her among its pages. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cynthia Erivo Calls Out Public’s ‘Annoyance’ Over Ariana Grande Friendship: ‘Why Are They Showing Emotion? How Dare They Cry!’
item.description: Cynthia Erivo is reflecting on the attention her friendship with “Wicked” co-star Ariana Grande received while on the press tour for the movie musical and its sequel. The theater star and singer has rocketed to greater heights of fame following Jon M. Chu’s adaptation of “Wicked,” which stars Erivo as the wicked witch Elphaba opposite […] Fuente: Variety.
item.dc:creator: Mya Copeland

item.title: Scientists count more than 2 million eels on one underwater mountain
item.description: Patience Seamount is an underwater mountain in Australia's Huon Marine Park off the coast of Tasmania. Every year, it is the site of an enormous gathering of basketwork eels (Diastobranchus capensis) for reasons unknown, although most likely to spawn. The numbers are huge, but they have never been quantified. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds celebrity digital twins may boost trust in customer service
item.description: Imagine losing your credit card, logging into your bank's website for help and being greeted by a virtual customer service representative who looks and sounds exactly like actor Hugh Jackman. The person helping you isn't actually the Hollywood star—it's his AI-powered digital twin. And new research suggests that familiar face could significantly improve how you perceive your customer service experience. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wiz’s CTO on PHP2Shell and the coming ‘vulnpocalypse’
item.description: The PHP scare may have faded from your feed, but the cleanup is far from over. Last week, two critical bugs in the open source language behind roughly 70% of websites left organizations scrambling to fix their systems, with some taking sites offline until the vulnerabilities could be patched. According to researchers who found the […] Fuente: TechCrunch.
item.dc:creator: Theresa Loconsolo

item.title: Gambling risks found among teens as young as 13
item.description: More than half (52.5%) of Americans ages 13 to 27 reported gambling in the past year, including 42.7% of teens ages 13 to 17, according to researchers at the Center for Gambling Studies at the Rutgers School of Social Work. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Artemis III SLS Core Stage Joins Boosters at Kennedy
item.description: NASA’s Artemis III SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is integrated alongside the twin solid rocket boosters on Oct. 28 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Technicians lifted the 212-foot rocket stage from the facility’s High Bay 2 using a one-of-a kind lifting beam designed […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Tiffany L. Fairley

item.title: How childhood experiences shape employment outcomes in India
item.description: Research led by the University of East Anglia (UEA) shows that childhood poverty, poor living conditions and gender can have lasting impacts on employment opportunities and earnings in India. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: UV scans uncover natural varnish that may have preserved ancient Chauvet Cave drawings
item.description: Tucked away inside a limestone cave in southeastern France lies some of the oldest artwork in existence. Known as Chauvet Cave, the site is so historically important—and fragile—that its location is kept secret and the cave is locked behind a huge steel door. And now, researchers have devised a technique to safely investigate these artworks and understand the natural varnish that has protected them for centuries. Their findings are published in the journal ACS Omega. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Supersonic waves could explain the strange orbits of hot Jupiters and Neptunes
item.description: Using advanced new simulations, a team of astronomers in the U.S. has developed a promising new theory for how giant, gaseous exoplanets migrate into stiflingly close orbits around their host stars. Led by J. J. Zanazzi at The Pennsylvania State University, the team showed how both massive "hot Jupiters" and smaller, Neptune-sized planets could migrate from distant, elliptical orbits as they release energy via dramatic shock waves in their outer atmospheres. Their results have been published in The Astrophysical Journal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US adults say craft and sustained commitment, not fame, separate creators from influencers
item.description: The creator economy is a growing global industry that Goldman Sachs Research reports could be worth $480 billion by 2027. But what is a creator, and what is the difference between a creator and an influencer, a celebrity or everyone else who posts online? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA University Challenge Ignites Trajectory of Drone Entrepreneur
item.description: Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge. Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jim Banke

item.title: Why hugs become memorable
item.description: A large-scale survey of adults in the U.K. shows that hugs are commonly remembered for comfort, support and understanding, according to a study published in PLOS One by Anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol, U.K., and colleagues. Notably, individual differences in empathy, attachment patterns in relationships, body perception and everyday hugging experiences were also related to the likelihood of remembering a hug for its positive emotional effect. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Eaton Fire may have exposed nearly 7 million people to elevated lead levels
item.description: Caltech scientists have published the first detailed analysis of the atmospheric particles in the smoke plume from the Eaton Fire that devastated much of the town of Altadena in Southern California's San Gabriel Valley and the surrounding areas in January 2025. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How to be happy: Tips from the pioneers of well being research
item.description: Earlier this year, we convened a meeting of some of the most influential figures in modern happiness research to discuss what they had learned in their 600 combined years of research and professional experience. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A spider named for Stephen Colbert has a genome about 50% larger than ours
item.description: Many spiders reach their maximum size about this time of year, having spent the summer eating, which helps explain their starring role in Halloween decorations. Researchers at the University of California, Davis, have found that one particular trapdoor spider, Aptostichus stephencolberti, which is about the size of a quarter, is big in another way: It has an outsized genome. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How political polarization creates business uncertainty
item.description: New research by a Florida State University professor in the Herbert Wertheim College of Business finds that America's increasingly polarized political system reaches far beyond the ballot box, creating greater uncertainty and higher costs for companies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Elementary school homework could be reinforcing educational inequality, study suggests
item.description: Homework set by elementary schools could be reinforcing educational inequalities by rewarding families who have more time and resources to spend helping their children, new research from the University of Manchester suggests. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How evolutionary biology became an unwilling ally of the manosphere
item.description: From steroid use to "bone smashing", the "looksmaxxing" movement is only the latest example of the manosphere's toxic hold on young people. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When simulations fall short, this spectrometer learns for itself
item.description: An NMR spectrometer can reveal molecular structure down to the atomic level, but weak signals limit what it can see. Now, Aarhus University researchers have used AI to let the spectrometer learn the best pulse sequence directly from the sample. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Selects 19 New Citizen Science Proposals in 2026
item.description: So far, 2026 has seen a flood of successes for volunteers who do NASA science, exemplifying NASA’s commitment to gold-standard science—transparent, reproducible and intrinsically collaborative. The Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project announced that their project volunteers have now discovered most of the known brown dwarfs, celestial objects that are similar to planets. The Zooniverse platform, […] Fuente: NASA.

item.description: Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA systems engineering team details Habitable Worlds Observatory mission architecture
item.description: Finding an Earth-like world beyond the solar system is the holy grail of exoplanet research, and the field has seen remarkable technological advances in detecting and studying exoplanets since the first confirmed exoplanet around a sun-like star was discovered in 1995. These advances include ground- and space-based telescopes, notably the James Webb Space Telescope. Although astronomers have already directly imaged some exoplanets, directly imaging Earth-like planets around sun-like stars remains a major technological challenge, primarily because these planets are extremely faint compared… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 2024 solar storm triggered ultrarelativistic electrons inside Earth's 'impenetrable barrier'
item.description: The Earth is surrounded by an invisible barrier that was thought to prevent highly energetic electrons from reaching closer to our planet. But in 2024, Japan's Arase space probe detected these electrons well inside the barrier. Now, research led by Nagoya University has found evidence that the electrons were accelerated locally rather than infiltrating from outer radiation belts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Webb Sees Turbulent Star Nursery
item.description: In this Webb image released on Oct. 22, 2026, we see a turbulent cauldron of star formation filled with dense clumps of gas. This region is named N159 and is located 161,000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the satellite galaxies orbiting the Milky Way galaxy. This region has a lower metallicity […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Refugees' experiences of loss shape their business ambitions
item.description: The severity of the losses refugees experience can shape the kinds of businesses they build in a new country, according to a qualitative study by Tilburg University researcher Kurian George and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Portable device accurately and rapidly detects PFAS in water
item.description: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are synthetic chemicals known for their exceptional resistance to degradation, earning them the nickname "forever chemicals." These persistent substances can accumulate in water, soil and living organisms, raising concerns about their potential impacts on human health and the environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can gravitational fields break and reconnect? Einstein's equations suggest they can
item.description: More than a century after Einstein first devised the equations that describe gravity, physicists are still finding new ways of interpreting them. Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, recently found a new way of looking at Einstein's equations that reveals a striking analogy with "magnetic reconnection" in plasmas, which occurs when magnetic field lines break and reconnect, powering explosive phenomena such as solar flares. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Europa: el calor del verano de 2026 dejó más de 50.000 muertos
item.description: Más de 50.000 personas murieron por causas relacionadas con el calor en las ciudades europeas durante el verano de 2026, según una nueva investigación científica. El estudio estima que alrededor de dos tercios de esos fallecimientos son atribuibles al calentamiento provocado por la actividad humana. Italia, Francia y España registraron las cifras más elevadas de mortalidad. Los investigadores advierten de que el balance podría ser aún mayor: el análisis abarca 854 áreas urbanas de 30 países, que representan aproximadamente el 40% de su población. ¿Qué revela este verano sobre el impacto del… Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: María Clara Calle Aguirre

item.title: Launch of global seed platform to tackle native seed bottleneck holding back nature restoration
item.description: On Oct. 13, the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (RBG Kew) launched the Seed Portal for Online Data (SeedPOD), a new open-access platform designed to tackle bottlenecks affecting global ecological restoration, by making native seed collections and the knowledge needed to grow them easier to discover. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Japan's genome-editing law sets a global ethics challenge
item.description: A Hiroshima University researcher contends that Japan's newly enacted law regulating human genome-edited embryos and germ cells marks a significant advance in the governance of reproductive genome editing. Tsutomu Sawai, professor at Hiroshima University's Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, praises the new law for defining prohibited activities and penalties for violation but also stresses the need for stronger international coordination to prevent the prohibitions from being circumvented by individuals seeking procedures abroad. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Against all expectations, researchers control the magnetic core of a single atom
item.description: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have succeeded in controlling the magnetism in the nucleus of a single atom with radio waves. This came as a surprise: until now, physicists believed that this nuclear spin could not be manipulated directly. The discovery could open up new possibilities for storing and reading quantum information. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nature-inspired additive could help protect living cells during freezing and thawing
item.description: In Australia, around 2,000 people are on the waiting list to receive an organ transplant, but thanks to new research being undertaken at the University of New England (UNE), this number could someday be significantly reduced. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
item.description: When a star like our sun grows old, it puffs up into a red giant that can gobble up its nearest planets. But Chinese astronomers say they have found three solar systems where planets should have been eaten this way yet somehow survived – a puzzle that could change how scientists picture Earth’s distant future. Using Nasa’s TESS space telescope, a team led by Qian Shengbang from Yunnan University showed that three Jupiter-like planets – each hugging an ageing star in the northern sky – had lived... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: A 60-year search is over: Chemists isolate long-elusive molecules with boron-oxygen triple bonds
item.description: In a new publication in the journal Nature Chemistry, chemists in professor Holger Braunschweig's team at the University of Würzburg, supported by computational work from the team of professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University in India, detail their discovery of a method for preparing and isolating a range of surprisingly stable oxoboranes—a challenge that has stood for over 60 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky—this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
item.description: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects? It's earwax. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Amber fossils reveal how ancient Australian landmass helped seed Southeast Asia's tropical forests
item.description: A landmass that broke away from northwestern Australia about 150 million years ago and drifted north for the next 100 million years helped lay the foundations for Southeast Asia's extraordinarily diverse tropical forests, new research has revealed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Indonesia's El Niño–driven peat fires are choking the region—and releasing centuries of stored carbon
item.description: Right now, people in parts of Indonesia are inhaling what may be the most polluted atmosphere on Earth. As the historically large 2026 El Niño intensifies, parts of Southeast Asia have been plunged into an air quality crisis of catastrophic proportions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Do spiders dream? Researchers studying spiders have found sleep patterns resembling REM sleep
item.description: A recent study on Australian jumping spiders has uncovered that these creatures undergo unique sleep stages, reminiscent of REM sleep. The observed sleep patterns, characterized by distinct periods of stillness interspersed with muscle movements and eye twitches, suggest that spiders possess more advanced sleep mechanisms than previously believed. Future research aims to explore their natural sleeping behaviors, offering insights into the links between sleep and cognitive processes across species. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: National parenting support strategy could strengthen Australia's efforts to protect children
item.description: Australia has no shortage of policies relating to children. In fact, these policies are often in the headlines. Billions of dollars are invested each year trying to improve outcomes for children and young people. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Parts of Tibetan Plateau's frozen ground are gaining ice despite warming
item.description: High on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, the ground stays frozen, with only the top few meters melting each summer. Although the region is warming about twice as fast as the global average, a new study finds that more than a third of its permafrost, mainly in the central plateau, has gained ice since 2000. Stronger westerly winds bring more rain and snow, which seeps into the ground in summer and freezes again in winter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Still looking for your Halloween costume? Try dressing up as the most terrifying thing in the universe.... Ver más
item.description: Still looking for your Halloween costume? Try dressing up as the most terrifying thing in the universe.... Ver más Tenemos problemas para reproducir este vídeo. Más información Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden defense mechanism in aging muscles that sacrifices strength to protect cells from damage. In mice, partially restoring a crucial molecule reversed signs of muscle wasting and prevented premature death, raising hopes for new treatments for age-related muscle decline. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: When consumers search 'cyclospora,' bagged salad sales take the hit
item.description: This year, the U.S. saw its highest annual count of confirmed Cyclospora cases, roughly 20,000, according to the CDC. New research published in Risk Analysis examines outbreaks from 2018 to 2022 and finds that the retail losses associated with these events vary with how much public attention the outbreak draws. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ants prioritize brain energy during starvation, echoing pattern seen in humans
item.description: The human brain accounts for roughly 2% of total body weight but uses approximately 20% of our body's energy. Relative to our body size, human brains are much larger than those of other mammals and take a lot of energy to keep humans going. The evolution of our unusually large "social brain" is thought to have given us advanced intelligence and enabled the formation of large, complex societies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New feed supplement addresses honey bee declines after blueberry pollination
item.description: Washington produces more blueberries than any other U.S. state, but farmers sometimes struggle to obtain honey bees to pollinate the plants and produce fruit. That's in part because beekeepers are reluctant to provide bees to blueberry farms, given that there have been increased—and mysterious—bee colony losses after blueberry pollination. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Smaller EV batteries, longer range? Scientists may have found a way
item.description: Scientists have developed a new technology that could make electric vehicle batteries smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting, potentially allowing cars to travel farther on a single charge. By borrowing precision manufacturing techniques from computer chip production, they found a way to prevent damaging lithium buildup that has held back next-generation batteries. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders
item.description: Researchers have discovered a surprising hidden ability in Europe's familiar black-and-yellow fire salamanders: they glow green and cyan under ultraviolet light. The mysterious fluorescence comes mainly from glands in their skin and their toxic secretions, which can continue glowing for more than 24 hours after being released. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a long-lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years, revealing a hidden chapter in Earth's tectonic history. The discovery sheds new light on the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Sound-levitated particles reveal how static charge builds up
item.description: When two objects touch and then separate, they can swap tiny amounts of electric charge, even if they are made from exactly the same material. This 'triboelectric effect' is the source of everyday static electricity, but it is still poorly understood in large samples of powder, where vast numbers of particles are constantly colliding with each other. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds heat waves speed snowmelt substantially, but rivers respond unevenly
item.description: A new study by researchers at Montana State University has found that heat waves substantially accelerate the melting rate of mountain snowpack; however, the resulting water doesn't necessarily produce an immediate increase in streamflow. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unos científicos desarrollan un dispositivo capaz de unir la luz de varios telescopios y lo probarán en Calar Alto, Almería
item.description: La astronomía ha evolucionado muchísimo en los últimos años. Cada vez se pueden captar objetos más difusos y lejanos , pero todo tiene un límite. Para llegar más lejos, es necesario que los telescopios puedan captar más luz. Eso se consigue con telescopios más grandes, pero, técnicamente hablando, es algo que tiene un límite. Por eso, la ciencia se centra también en la búsqueda de formas de combinar la luz de muchos telescopios pequeños en una sola señal que los instrumentos puedan manipular. Justamente eso es lo que pretende hacer un equipo internacional de científicos, dirigido por el… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Fishmeal alternative aims to protect marine wildlife from overfishing
item.description: Technology that transforms organic waste into animal feed could help ease an overreliance on fishmeal in aquaculture. University of Queensland researchers have developed a production process that converts organic waste into biogas to grow a high-protein alternative to fish feed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Luxury round-the-world cruise ends abruptly as fuel costs skyrocket
item.description: Cruise operator Villa Vie Residences said it would disembark passengers and crew, and restructure its business due to soaring fuel costs. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: Dead tree branches rise and fall with changing humidity, laser scans reveal
item.description: Dead tree branches are by no means static but move throughout the day. Geoinformatics researchers at Heidelberg University tracked these movements in a study conducted in cooperation with the Finnish Geospatial Research Institute (FGI). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between Earth's opposite poles that may help explain how the planet plunged into past ice ages. New research suggests that as massive ice sheets expanded across the Northern Hemisphere, they cooled Atlantic Ocean waters that eventually traveled south toward Antarctica. This cooling may have disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, allowing the ocean to absorb and store more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, further cooling the planet. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Machine learning simulations reveal how plastic transforms into hard carbon
item.description: In a new study published in Chemical Science, researchers from the University of Oxford's Department of Chemistry have used machine learning simulations to trace how a common polymer transforms into hard carbon, revealing the atomic-scale processes that give this technologically important material its disordered structure. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why do people self-harm? The mind-body divide might hold some clues
item.description: In Finnish lore, the goddess Kivutar stashes away pain in a mountain for safekeeping. And yet she's also a healer, channeling it into rocks or boiling it down into a less potent form in a huge vat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon
item.description: NASA’s Artemis I mission has revealed that cosmic radiation near the Moon is higher than in Earth orbit, but not by as much as scientists might expect. Tiny experimental detectors also uncovered surprising details about how radiation passes through the human body, offering valuable insights for future lunar exploration. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: U.S. moves to weaken methane limits on oil and gas producers
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump announced Tuesday a sweeping rollback of rules that stop oil and gas producers from emitting methane, a greenhouse gas superpollutant. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cyclone eases after lashing India coast, no deaths reported
item.description: Ferocious winds and torrential rain lashed India's southeastern coast after a cyclone made landfall on Wednesday, but officials said there were no initial reports of deaths and the storm later began to ease. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Comets probably didn't seed life on Earth after all, new study suggests
item.description: The theory that comets delivered the molecular building blocks for life on Earth is a long-standing one, since comets are known to carry many of these molecules. However, a new study challenges this idea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Antarctica’s “Doomsday Glacier” could raise sea levels twice as much as predicted
item.description: Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier may be melting twice as much as previously predicted, even without additional global warming. Scientists discovered that warm ocean water is penetrating miles beneath the ice, weakening its foundations and accelerating its retreat. A new model predicts that the glacier could add up to 30 millimeters to global sea levels by 2100, with a 60% chance of losing a crucial stabilizing ridge. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Kimmy Kim ha comentado: Yes not for Halloween BUT for Hollywood indeed
item.description: Are you stepping into a spacesuit this week? We are — but not for Halloween! Tune in on Thursday, Oct. 29, to watch NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA... Fuente: NASA.

item.title: EEUU acaba de revelar que China tiene un avión secreto orbitando en el espacio desde seis hace años
item.description: Durante años, una fotografía tomada en el espacio alimentó las sospechas de que China había conseguido desarrollar su propia versión de uno de los vehículos militares más secretos de Estados Unidos. La imagen circulaba por internet, había aparecido incluso en una presentación de la Fuerza Espacial estadounidense y nadie había confirmado públicamente qué mostraba exactamente. Ahora, un informe de la inteligencia militar de Washington ha resuelto el misterio: Pekín dispone de un avión espacial reutilizable extraordinariamente parecido al X-37B estadounidense . Y los detalles que han salido a la… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Experts defer to AI in decision-making, Anthropic study finds
item.description: Professional analysts chose options that matched AI assistant's preference 86 percent of the time, research finds. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.description: Written by Lucy Lim, Planetary Scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Earth planning date: Friday, Oct. 16, 2026 Following the Basque Lakes drill campaign, Curiosity has returned to a spot just a few meters away from the “Chiu Chiu” block to conduct our next drill campaign. “Chiu Chiu” itself wasn’t a good candidate for […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: After 1,600 years, researchers recreate the colour-changing glass of a Roman masterpiece
item.description: A team of researchers has made a groundbreaking achievement by replicating the color-shifting glass of the ancient Roman Lycurgus Cup. Created 1,600 years ago, this unique glass displays stunning optical effects thanks to its tiny gold and silver nanoparticles. Their rigorous experimentation with both ancient and modern techniques opens doors for scientific advancements, extending beyond mere artistic creation. A modern sculpture inspired by this historic artifact will soon be unveiled. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks
item.description: A national monument since the 1920s, Chiricahua is America’s newest national park. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength
item.description: A new clinical trial suggests that a simple daily fiber supplement could significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, improve muscle strength, and make the body less sensitive to pain. Researchers discovered that the benefits may be linked to changes in gut bacteria and the hormone GLP-1, revealing a promising new approach to arthritis relief. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: MapInsights helps police trainees learn the territory
item.description: In early 2026, the University of Illinois Division of Public Safety was facing a challenge. It had 11 security guards it planned to convert to community service officers, which meant they would change from being based in one building to working a whole beat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
item.description: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
